title: Odd engagements: Picayune, a bad piano and Frank Curety
summary: He recounts playing in decrepit halls, and pianist Frank Curety who tuned pianos and played the phantom bass.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Oh, I wouldn't want to. I wouldn't know. A musician is bound to have strange experiences. I played places I was afraid to go in. For instance, the man in Miami from Charmpton Beach, which is Patterson, Louisiana. You heard of him? Are you available? Yes. Some of you are particular. I demand a deposit. I drive up to the place, I say, it can't be possible. But after they turn the lights on and all the society people come in there, it's a beautiful place. They've got a good band and a good crowd. It's the same as the auditorium under Roosevelt. It's no different. But it's an unpainted building and you're afraid you say, well, I played in Picayune one night in the dead of winter. They didn't have a windowpane in the windows. They were all broken off and the kids, and the guy had to go screw fuses in before we could get some lights. And I said to the man in the oil station, where is this dance being held? He said, down, a little piece down the road. I said, this must be it. And I'll look in there. And gee, some of the flooring was down and some was up. But I had been engaged by the postmaster, who was a man of integrity. I didn't have to work. I'm telling you, we were all waiting in the dark until they screwed the fuses in. Oh, I played places where we couldn't use the piano. We turned the back of the piano to the audience, they never knew whether we were a pianist or not. He didn't play it. I told him, don't you dare touch it all on a tune. I played one time at the Arabian High School. They wrote the piano around. It was white. They had used it for chicken roots. It was white. But I happened to have Frank Curety with me then as a pianist who was a very fine, legitimate piano player. I had good rhythm. Frank, I love Frank. We used to. But he loved bolts and motors and he'd come with his fingernails full of grime. So I said, there's only one thing we can do, Frank, is cut your nails down to the quick and scrub it with some lava soap or something like that. Because he'd forget about the job and come be working on his motor. And then people look at him, he'd be in the stands, especially if he's a good one, you know? So Frank says, what will I do? I said, well let's see if we can use it. If it's too much out of tune, I'd throw it out. I wasn't going to have my saxophones all out of tune. I'd rather have one piano out than have nine men all out of tune. And Frank used to carry a tuning hammer with him. Oh, he was the piano player you'd have. Because when we used to play in the patio room, the moment we walk in, the manager sent up a red tray or drink. Why? Because you're going to get a free piano tuning job from CUNY. Because one day we went and the pedals were all on the bumper. CUNY was under the piano, Martin was sitting at the piano trying to fix the pedals. And he wanted to do a job, you know? Well that's a conscientious person, isn't it? So he carried a tuning hammer. And when we get, he tuned the middle register. So I guess the next piano player, when he started to go down up high or down low, he found out he was about a quarter of a tone out from the middle register. But Frank would stay in the middle register and wouldn't devote too much time to the bass because we had a bass. Let the bass man play the right bass notes, you know? I mean he wouldn't reach down. He'd play the phantom bass. They call that a phantom bass. They don't hit anything. It's just moving the hand. Nobody thinks he's playing. He can hit the damn thing. I remember one night, I used to play at the Gulf Coast Military Academy. It's a school for boys, a preparatory school. You've heard of it, haven't you?
